claims.claim: Aramini reports as general critical consensus that Wolfe leaves certain resolutions out of the text for the reader to infer.
claims.source: Marc Anthony Aramini, 'Does It Mean? Gene Wolfe: Perverse Puzzle Maker', PhD dissertation, University of Nevada Las Vegas, May 2019
claims.quote: Wolfe leaves out certain resolutions which are left to the reader

claims.claim: Aramini reports Peter Wright's contrary position that many details in Wolfe's primary narrative are distractions rather than clues.
claims.source: Peter Wright, Attending Daedalus (Liverpool University Press, 2003), summarised by Marc Aramini in his UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: many of the details included in the primary narrative

claims.claim: Aramini reports Wright's finding that Wolfe's translator persona makes deliberate mistranslations and substitutions inside the Latro books.
claims.source: Peter Wright, Attending Daedalus (Liverpool University Press, 2003), p. 188, quoted by Marc Aramini in his UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: explicit mistranslations and substitutions by the translator Wolfe

claims.claim: A passage of Wolfe's own fiction reproduced in Aramini's dissertation states that what is not said can be important but what is said matters more.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Sword of the Lictor, p. 182, quoted within Peter Wright's argument as reproduced in Marc Aramini's UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: What is not said can be important

claims.claim: Aramini argues that Wolfe builds his Latro narrative on the Herodotean model of an account that blends history, myth and rumour.
claims.source: Marc Anthony Aramini, UNLV dissertation, May 2019

claims.claim: A passage of Wolfe's The Wizard Knight reproduced in Aramini's dissertation describes a past that survives only as memories and as records nobody reads or can read.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Wizard Knight, p. 39, quoted in Marc Aramini's UNLV dissertation, 2019
claims.quote: records nobody reads, and records nobody can read

claims.claim: Clute reports that the large cast of The Book of the Short Sun speaks in dozens of distinct dialects and accents, each rendered with care.
claims.source: John Clute, 'It Is Becoming to Grapple with This Book', Excessive Candour column, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: dozens of different dialects and accents spoken by the huge cast

claims.claim: Clute identifies Wolfe's refusal to restate a difficult story in easy terms as one of the things the reader must struggle with.
claims.source: John Clute, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: refusal to unpack in easy terms

claims.claim: Clute locates the moral quality of Wolfe's central character in the details rather than in any statement about him.
claims.source: John Clute, Science Fiction Weekly issue 197, 29 January 2001
claims.quote: that goodness is in the details

claims.claim: Clute argues that every word in Wolfe's stories is deliberate, so that no sentence can be slurred over by the reader.
claims.source: John Clute, review of The Best of Gene Wolfe, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: every word he wrote was meant

claims.claim: Clute states that Wolfe did not write metaphors into his text, or wrote only metaphors to which a literal meaning could be attached.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: Wolfe did not create metaphors in his text

claims.claim: Clute says the nearest Wolfe normally comes to metaphor is letting one of his characters tell a lie.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: the closest Wolfe normally gets to metaphor is when he
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Clute argues Wolfe wrote neither thematics nor allegory but the thing itself.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: he did not write allegory, he wrote the thing itself

claims.claim: Clute says Wolfe's stories cannot be paraphrased for meaning because they only make sense once the manner of their telling is understood.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: stories that only make sense when it is understood how

claims.claim: Clute describes the surface of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as a fluent and seemingly translucent style.
claims.source: John Clute, SCI FI Wire, 6 April 2009
claims.quote: written in a fluent, seemingly translucent style
claims.page: paragraph on The Fifth Head of Cerberus
